info.disambiguation: American singer and songwriter, “King of Soul”
info.bio:
Sam Cooke, cantante de soul y gospel nacido en Mississippi el 22 de enero de 1931. Está considerado uno de los pioneros de la música soul, siendo una de las grandes influencias del pop, el rhythm and blues y el neo soul.

Para algunos está considerado como «Rey del Soul» (título que comparte con Otis Redding), y con el paso del tiempo el hecho de que tuviera casi la treintena de hits entre 1957 y 1965 ha hecho a muchos pensar que realmente es uno de los padres del soul.

scenes.name: Soul y R&B
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: El 1 de enero de 1966 el Top 3 estadounidense lo formaban «The Sound of Silence», «We Can Work It Out» y el «I Got You (I Feel Good)» de James Brown: discos futuristas los tres. A finales de mes Otis Redding se acercaba al Top 10 británico con su versión de «My Girl» de los Temptations.

scenes.name: Derechos civiles: de Selma a la Marcha contra el Miedo
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: Cada avance llegó con palizas y asesinatos televisados: Little Rock, los Freedom Riders, Birmingham, los tres activistas muertos en el Freedom Summer de 1964. El «Bloody Sunday» del puente Edmund Pettus en Selma (marzo de 1965) empujó a Johnson a la Ley de Derecho al Voto, firmada el 6 de agosto; Malcolm X había sido asesinado en febrero. Cinco días después ardía Watts: seis días de disturbios, treinta y cuatro muertos, la rebelión de un gueto zonificado para la pobreza. La no violencia de Martin Luther King se resquebrajaba y el SNCC, más joven y radical, se alejaba de la SCLC. Muy pocos discos negros hablaban de los derechos civiles («A Change Is Gonna Come» de Sam Cooke, «Keep on Pushing» y «People Get Ready» de los Impressions; «Mississippi Goddam» de Nina Simone fue prohibido), pero el público oía mensajes en «Dancing in the Street», «Shotgun» o «Nowhere to Run», metáforas de lo que aún no se podía decir. El 5 de junio de 1966 James Meredith empezó su Marcha contra el Miedo de Memphis a Jackson; al segundo día le dispararon y los líderes de todos los grupos la continuaron juntos por última vez.

scenes.name: De los derechos civiles al Black Power
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: «No se puede hablar del funk sin hablar de la Revolución Negra» (Shock G). Las sentadas, los Freedom Rides y la Marcha sobre Washington de 1963 llevaron el gospel a la calle («A Change Is Gonna Come», «Keep on Pushing»), pero pese a las leyes la masa negra apenas notó cambios. Malcolm X habló por los desposeídos y su asesinato en 1965 dejó un vacío: «It was a funky deal» (Etheridge Knight). Vinieron Watts (con el DJ Magnificent Montague pinchando «Burn, Baby, Burn»), el grito de «Black Power» en la marcha de Meredith de 1966, el SNCC sin blancos, los Panteras Negras de Huey Newton y Bobby Seale en Oakland (armados en el Capitolio de California en 1967, «la mayor amenaza» para Hoover), Newark y Detroit en 1967, los disturbios tras el asesinato de King en 1968, los puños de Tommie Smith y John Carlos en México y el «ningún Vietcong me llamó nigger» de Muhammad Ali. Futuros músicos funk (Marshall Jones de los Ohio Players, Bootsy en Cincinnati, Mudbone Cooper en Baltimore) tiraron piedras en los disturbios: la universidad de la calle. «Say It Loud – I’m Black and I’m Proud» de James Brown convirtió «black» en elogio; «Black Is Beautiful» invirtió siglos de lenguaje y hasta «funky» se reivindicó. Esa libertad de redefinir lo negro fue la incubadora del funk.

scenes.name: El soul: gospel y R&B
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: El soul fue el comienzo de la síntesis de la América negra: el R&B popular con la moral del gospel, el sábado por la noche y el domingo por la mañana en uno. Lo originó en los cincuenta Ray Charles, que convirtió «My Jesus Is All the World to Me» en «I Got a Woman»; Clinton llama a «What’d I Say» el disco más funky jamás hecho. De la iglesia salieron Aretha Franklin, Sam Cooke, Al Green, Johnnie Taylor, Joe Tex, los Staple Singers, Donny Hathaway o Larry Graham. Jerry Wexler dejó a Aretha arreglar sus temas en Muscle Shoals y «Respect» (1967) se volvió la metáfora de los anhelos de todo un pueblo; con ella la reina del soul elevó toda la música negra. El mismo año salió «Cold Sweat», casi el primer groove funk, estallaron los peores disturbios y murieron Otis y Coltrane; los Impressions cantaban «We’re a Winner». Hasta «Say It Loud» (1968) el soul expresó la unidad negra; después vinieron los poetas revolucionarios (Watts Prophets, Gil Scott-Heron, Last Poets) y el black rock.

scenes.name: Curtis Mayfield
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: El faro del soul funky independiente. Inspirado por Sam Cooke, uno de los primeros negros en controlar su producción, fundó Curtom en 1968 al frente de los Impressions y al irse en solitario (1970) llevó su independencia y su comentario social a temas largos y experimentales: «(Don’t Worry) If There’s a Hell Below, We’re All Going to Go», «We the People Who Are Darker Than Blue», «Mighty Mighty (Spade and Whitey)», «I Plan to Stay a Believer» (veinte millones a diez dólares por cabeza salvarían al niño del gueto). Su voz tierna desarmaba al oyente ante visiones callejeras implacables. La banda sonora de Super Fly (1972) unió conciencia social y estilo callejero: elegancia de terciopelo y realismo, el ideal de la comunidad negra de principios de los setenta.

scenes.name: Antes del diluvio
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: La «edad oscura» del rock'n'roll: los rebeldes son sustituidos por ídolos adolescentes educados y el Brill Building devuelve el poder a los compositores profesionales. Pero en esos años se incuban la revolución futura: la guitarra fuzz de Link Wray, los bailes de moda (el twist), el rock instrumental de guitarras (Duane Eddy, Ventures, Shadows), el calipso y el primer ska, el doo-wop más inventivo (Coasters, Drifters, Five Royales), el nacimiento del soul (Sam Cooke, Ray Charles, Motown, Stax), el estudio como instrumento de Joe Meek y el surf de los Beach Boys y del «muro de sonido» de Phil Spector.

podcast.title: Ed Sullivan Show Debacle (1957)
podcast.body: Sam Cooke experienced a "catastrophic" appearance on the Ed Sullivan Show, where he was accidentally cut off halfway through a song, despite his version of "You Send Me" being a massive hit. "You Send Me...went to number one on both the R and B and the pop charts, despite a catastrophic appearance on the Ed Sullivan show which accidentally caught him off halfway through a song."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty: "You Send Me" by Sam Cooke

podcast.title: Seeds of Downfall (1957)
podcast.body: By the close of 1957, despite being at the peak of his commercial success, Sam Cooke's relentless pursuit of career control and personal gain at the expense of others had laid the groundwork for his future downfall, causing pain to those who had supported him, including his gospel groups and many women. "He was upsetting all the right people with his desire to have control of his own career, but he was also hurting a lot of other people along the way."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty: "You Send Me" by Sam Cooke

podcast.title: Delayed for 1962 UK Tour
podcast.body: Sam Cooke, who was the second-billed star for Little Richard's October 1962 UK tour, was delayed and unable to make the first show, which was deemed "a bit of a disaster." "Sam Cook, who was the second build star for the show, was delayed and couldn't make the first show, which was a bit of a disaster."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 54: Keep A Knockin

podcast.title: Behavior Towards Women
podcast.body: Cook was known for his "far less admirable" behavior towards women, getting married in 1953 but having at least one child with another woman whom he abandoned. He consistently engaged in infidelity while touring, leading to multiple pregnancies with different women he refused to acknowledge or support. "But Cook treated women the same way he treated the groups he was in. Use them for as long as they've got something you want, and then immediately cast them aside once it became inconvenient."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty: "You Send Me" by Sam Cooke

podcast.title: Central Avenue Music Scene Involvement
podcast.body: While waiting for Keen Records to get set up, Sam Cooke became deeply involved in the Central Avenue music scene in Los Angeles, regularly interacting with figures like Gaynell Hodge, Jesse Belvin, Dutti Williams, Guggi Renne, and John Dolphin within the LA R&B community. "Sam made himself firmly a part of the central avenue music scene, hanging around with Gaynell Hodge, Jesse Belvin, Dutti Williams, Guggi Renne, John Dolphin, and everyone else who was part of the LAR and B community."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty: "You Send Me" by Sam Cooke

podcast.title: Controversial Application of Father's Maxims
podcast.body: Cooke rigidly applied his father's advice about self-interest to all aspects of his life, demonstrating a disregard for the feelings and well-being of others, yet his immense talent and charm often led even those he hurt to defend him. "He was taking his father's maxims about only looking after yourself, and applying them to every aspect of life, with no regard to who it hurt."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Early Life and Religious Upbringing
podcast.body: Sam Cooke was one of seven children born to Reverend Charles Cook and Annie May. His father, a Reverend, trained all five performing children as singers from a very early age, forming the group The Singing Children who regularly performed in Chicago-area churches. "Young Sam was taught religion by his father, but he was also taught that there was no prohibition in the Bible against worldly success."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty: "You Send Me" by Sam Cooke

podcast.title: Father's Maxims for Success
podcast.body: Reverend Cook instilled two core principles in Sam that would significantly shape his life: the importance of striving for excellence in everything ("if a thing's worth doing, it's worth doing properly") and a ruthless pursuit of personal advancement ("you do whatever is necessary to give yourself the best possible life and don't worry about who you step on to do it"). "And the second was that you do whatever is necessary to give yourself the best possible life and don't worry about who you step on to do it."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: First Rock and Roll Era Musician Murdered
podcast.body: Sam Cooke, a renowned soul singer, was murdered on December 11, 1964. He sustained a gunshot wound to the chest when Bertha Franklin, the manager of the Hossie End of Motel on South Central Los Angeles, claimed he attacked her, asserting it was in self-defense. Despite her claim, many questions about the case persist even today. "He took a gunshot wound to the chest when Bertha Franklin, the manager of the Hossie end of Motel on South Central Los Angeles, said he attacked her."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rock Stars Who Were Murdered

podcast.title: Gospel to Pop Transition
podcast.body: In the mid-1950s, Sam Cooke was deliberating whether to transition from gospel music to secular pop, a decision he ultimately made with the number one hit "You Send Me" in 1957. His successful crossover inspired his friend Aretha Franklin to also pursue pop music as she approached her 18th birthday. "Inspired in part by her friend Sam Cook, as Aretha Franklin approached her 18th birthday, she decided she too wanted to record pop music."

podcast.title: Keen Records Formation
podcast.body: Sam Cooke and Bumps Blackwell took "You Send Me," "Summertime," and other recordings to a new label called Keen Records, which released them as its very first release after Blackwell's departure from Specialty Records. "But Cooke and Blackwell were free to take you send me summertime and the rest, to a new label that wanted them for its first release. Keen."

podcast.title: Mentorship and Betrayal within Gospel
podcast.body: While a member of the Highway QC's, the group was mentored by R.B. Robinson of The Soul Stirrers, who helped them secure better gigs. Unknown to the QC's, Robinson was actually training Sam Cooke to replace R.H. Harris as the lead singer of The Soul Stirrers, causing heartbreak for the QC's when Cooke left. "Robinson would train them and help them get better gigs, and the QCs became convinced they were headed for the big time."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty: "You Send Me" by Sam Cooke

podcast.title: Pivotal Role in Little Richard's Comeback
podcast.body: Sam Cooke, at the height of his success and an "astonishing live performer," played a crucial role in inspiring Little Richard's return to rock and roll during the 1962 UK tour. Cooke's manager, J.W. Alexander, advised promoter Don Arden to let Cooke perform, knowing that Richard's competitive nature would compel him to "up his game" after witnessing Cooke's powerful set. "Cook was at the height of his success at this point and he was an astonishing live performer and so when he went out on stage and closed the first half including an insendiary performance of twist in the night away that left the audience applauding through the intermission Richard knew he had to up his game."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 54: Keep A Knockin

podcast.title: R&B Chart Strategy
podcast.body: During the early 1960s, Sam Cooke achieved mass appeal with "percolating jams" that successfully merged pop and R&B elements. This style contrasted with Columbia Records' approach to Aretha Franklin, who was deemed "too gritty for the pop market, not earthy enough for R&B." "Aretha's gospel-trained friend was scoring with percolating jams that found a mass appeal midpoint between pop and R&B."

podcast.title: Retroactive Genre Re-labeling
podcast.body: Sam Cooke was widely considered "the greatest rock and roll singer in the world" by figures like Muhammad Ali at the time, with nobody questioning this classification. However, in modern contexts, his music is retroactively re-labeled and primarily discussed as soul, illustrating a trend where music by black artists is re-categorized over time. "at the time absolutely nobody would have questioned Cook being called rock and roll, but these days he would only be talked about as a soul singer."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 32: "I Got A Woman" by Ray Charles

podcast.title: Royalty Evasion Tactic
podcast.body: To prevent Art Rupe, who still held his songwriting contract, from collecting royalties on "You Send Me," Sam Cooke falsely attributed the song's authorship to his brother, LC Cook. This led to legal action initiated by Rupe against Cooke. "Sam was still signed to Roup's company as a songwriter, and so he'd put You Send Me in the name of his brother, LC, so Roup wouldn't get any royalties."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty: "You Send Me" by Sam Cooke

podcast.title: Solo Contract and Royalty Disputes
podcast.body: Sam Cooke's solo contract with Specialty Records only offered him one-third of the royalties that The Soul Stirrers had received as a group, prompting him to push for a greater share. This perceived "greed" angered label head Art Rupe, who believed artists should not receive more than one cent per record sold. "Cooke discovered that his solo contract only paid him a third of the royalties that the soul-sturers had been getting as a group, he started pushing for a great to share of the money."

xref.body: John Lennon was the first household name from the world of rock music to be murdered since Sam Cooke in 1964. His death marked a significant tragedy in rock history. "And Lennon, believe it or not, was the first household name from the world of rock to be murdered since Sam Cook in 1964."
